newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac summons politicians, early French poll seen.
newsitem.headline: Chirac summons politicians, early French poll seen.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac on Monday launched the procedure for calling an early parliamentary election by summoning French political leaders for manadatory consultations before a planned broadcast to the nation on Monday night.

The president planned separate meetings with Prime Minister Alain Juppe and the leaders of both houses of parliament, his office announced, amid expectations that he would call a snap poll for late May or early June, nine months ahead of schedule.

The consultations are required by the constitution before the president dissolves the National Assembly. Radio stations said Chirac had booked 10 minutes broadcasting time on Monday night to make an announcement.

The president's office has steadfastly refused comment on early election speculation, but cabinet ministers interviewed on talk shows all spoke on the assumption that the decision was certain and an announcement imminent.
The only uncertainty was whether the two-round election would be held on May 25 and June 1 or June 1 and 8.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told Europe 1 radio there were economic advantages to bringing forward the election due next March, since investment decisions were being delayed because of political uncertainty.

Industry Minister Franck Borotra said France needed to clear the decks with an election ahead of major decisions on European integration, including the selection in April or May 1998 of the first countries to qualify for a single European currency.

A SOFRES institute opinion poll published by the daily Le Figaro suggested the ruling centre-right coalition, which controls 478 of the Assembly's 577 seats, would lose about 150 seats but keep a comfortable overall majority.
It forecast the extreme-right National Front would capture 14.6 percent of the vote but win only two or three seats.

Pundits said Chirac wanted to get the election out of the way now rather than have to campaign next year at a time of possibly unpopular austerity measures to qualify France for the single European currency.
Even before Chirac fired the starter's gun, electioneering erupted in earnest on Sunday.

Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin said in a feisty television interview that he would reject tougher austerity if it were required to meet the criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Testing out his likely campaign themes, Jospin said an early poll would be "an admission of failure" by Juppe's government and the Left would offer an alternative strategy based on shorter working hours and a revival of economic growth.

"If the government had any confidence in the success of its policy, it would calmly wait for elections in a year," Jospin said, adding that Chirac was also worried about corruption probes rocking the ruling centre-right parties.
Communist party leader Robert Hue, who has demanded a referendum on a single currency, said Jospin's shift to a more critical stance on EMU was "undoubtedly a positive evolution".
But Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said Jospin was "manifestly embarrassed" by the prospect of an election and dismissed Socialist policies as archaic.

The daily Le Monde said Prime Minister Alain Juppe would set out campaign policies on Tuesday, including austerity moves such as speeding up tax cuts and limiting the role of the state, to enable France to qualify for EMU.
The president's mandate would not be directly affected by the vote. Elected in 1995, Chirac has five more years to serve. But a left-wing victory could make him a premature lame duck.
